keyTakeaways: SurtitleLive uses on-demand runtime delivery so the official viewer avoids loading a full plaintext script bundle up front.
Runtime subtitle content is delivered as encrypted segments and decrypted in browser memory for display.
Temporary bearer tokens, expiry windows, and server-side revocation controls help limit how long viewer access remains useful.
These controls reduce casual copying and uncontrolled access risk; they are not DRM or a promise of absolute copy protection.

faq.question: How does SurtitleLive reduce casual script copying?
faq.answer: The Official Viewer loads encrypted runtime segments on demand around the current cue instead of presenting the whole script as one readable browser payload at entry time.

faq.question: Can SurtitleLive guarantee that a script can never be copied?
faq.answer: No. Digital delivery cannot prevent screenshots, cameras, OCR, or custom clients with valid access. SurtitleLive should be treated as risk reduction, not absolute copy protection.

faq.question: What happens if a viewer link needs to be restricted?
faq.answer: Runtime access can be limited through temporary bearer tokens, configured expiry windows, and server-side revocation for new or renewed runtime requests.

faq.question: How is data protected in transit?
faq.answer: Connections use HTTPS/TLS, and runtime delivery uses encrypted runtime segments as part of a layered security model that also includes access scoping and operational controls.

glossary.definition: A small encrypted subtitle unit requested around show progress instead of a full plaintext script bundle.
The scoped browser session used by an intended audience viewer.
A server-side control that can limit new or renewed runtime access after a concern is detected.
A security goal that lowers practical copying and uncontrolled access risk without claiming absolute prevention.
